author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Most parents who search for a Class 2 maths book PDF are really after two things: a clear sense of what a seven-year-old is meant to learn this year, and something to practise it with at home. A good textbook — whether it is from Oxford University Press, an NCERT title, or your school's chosen series — answers the first. It rarely answers the second on its own, and that gap is where most children quietly fall behind.

So before you download anything, here is what a strong Class 2 maths book should cover, chapter by chapter, followed by how I would actually use it at home and why a book alone is almost never enough.

What a good Class 2 maths book covers

The syllabus is fairly settled across boards and publishers. If a book skips one of these, treat it as a warning sign rather than a lighter workload.

Numbers up to 1000

Class 1 ends around 100. Class 2 stretches to 1000, and the real lesson hiding inside those big numbers is place value — understanding that in 342 the 3 means three hundreds, the 4 means four tens, and the 2 means two ones. A child who can read and build three-digit numbers with tens-and-ones blocks is set up for everything that follows. One who has only learned to recite them is not.

Addition and subtraction with regrouping

This is the heavy lifting of the year. Adding 47 + 38 means the ones (7 + 8 = 15) spill over, so you carry a ten. Subtracting 52 − 27 means you cannot take 7 from 2, so you borrow a ten. Carrying and borrowing — regrouping — is where Class 2 children most often stumble, and it is exactly where a book gives you the method but only practice makes it stick.

The first times tables

Class 2 introduces multiplication as repeated addition — three groups of four is 4 + 4 + 4 — and usually the tables of 2, 5 and 10 to start. These three are chosen deliberately: they build the fastest and give a child early confidence before the trickier tables arrive in Class 3.

Fractions, measurement, money and time

A rounded book also introduces simple fractions (half and quarter of a shape or a group), measurement of length and weight in standard units, Indian money — adding rupees and paise, making change for a fifty-rupee note — and telling time to the hour and half-hour. Data handling appears too, usually as simple picture graphs (pictographs) where children count objects in a chart and answer questions about them.

How to use the book and practice together at home

Downloading a PDF is the easy part. Getting value from it takes a small routine. Here is the pattern that works with the families I have taught.

  • Read the worked example together first. Do not hand the book over cold. Sit with your child, read the one solved sum the chapter always gives, and talk through each step out loud.
  • Do two or three questions with them, not for them. Let them hold the pencil. Your job is to ask ‘what comes next?’ not to supply the answer.
  • Then let them work alone on a fresh set. This is the step a single textbook usually cannot support — most books give four or five practice sums per idea, and regrouping needs twenty. This is where a dedicated worksheet earns its place.
  • Mark it together the same day. A wrong answer spotted today is a lesson; the same mistake found next week is a habit.

Ten focused minutes a day beats an hour on Sunday. At this age consistency matters far more than length.

Why worksheets matter alongside any textbook

Here is the honest limitation of every Class 2 maths book, Oxford included: a textbook is built to teach a concept once, then move on. It has to fit a whole year between two covers, so it cannot give the sheer repetition that carrying, borrowing and the 2, 5 and 10 tables actually demand. A child usually understands regrouping the first day and forgets it by the weekend — not because the book was poor, but because five practice sums cannot build a reflex.

That is the specific job of a worksheet: same idea, many varied questions, with an answer key so you can check work without solving every sum yourself. Think of the textbook as the lesson and the worksheet as the training ground. You need both.

Covering the whole year's syllabusTargeting the one topic your child struggles with

A quick word on the PDF itself

Prefer the official source. Boards and publishers put their own material online, and NCERT offers its Class 2 mathematics book free and legally on its site. Downloading scanned copies of copyrighted Oxford titles from random file-sharing pages is both risky and unfair to the people who wrote them. If your school prescribes an Oxford book, buy or borrow the real thing and pair it with free or low-cost practice sheets — that combination costs little and works better than any single download.

Check where your child stands

Below is a short, free quiz pitched exactly at the Class 2 syllabus above — place value, regrouping, the early tables, fractions, money and time. Let your child try it, then read the explanations together for anything they miss. When you want longer written practice, the printable Class 2 workbook at the end gives graded questions on every one of these topics with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Class 2 Maths Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions covering place value, regrouping, the 2, 5 and 10 tables, fractions, money and time. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Class 2 maths across the year's core topics

questions.q: In the number 452, what does the digit 4 stand for?
questions.explanation: In 452 the 4 is in the hundreds place, so it means 4 hundreds, that is 400.
7 + 8 = 15, so write 5 and carry 1 ten. Then 4 + 3 + 1 = 8 tens. The answer is 85.
You cannot take 7 from 2, so borrow a ten: 12 - 7 = 5. Then 4 - 2 = 2 tens. The answer is 25.
5 x 4 means five groups of four, or 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 20.

questions.q: Which of these is the same as 4 + 4 + 4?
questions.explanation: Three groups of four is 3 x 4, which equals 12.
Half means splitting into two equal parts. 8 shared into two parts gives 4 each.

questions.q: You buy a pencil for 15 rupees and give a 20-rupee note. How much change do you get back?
The clock shows the hour hand halfway between 3 and 4, and the minute hand on 6. What is the time?
questions.explanation: The minute hand on 6 means half past. The hour hand just past 3 makes it half past 3.

faq.q: Is the Oxford Class 2 maths book better than NCERT?
faq.a: Both cover the same core syllabus — numbers to 1000, regrouping, early tables, fractions, money and time. Oxford titles tend to have more colour and context; NCERT is free, legal and thorough. Use whichever your school prescribes, and add practice sheets to either.

faq.q: Where can I legally download a Class 2 maths book PDF?
faq.a: NCERT publishes its Class 2 mathematics book free on its official website. For Oxford or other publisher titles, buy or borrow the real book rather than downloading scanned copies from file-sharing sites, which are unreliable and infringe copyright.

faq.q: What maths should a Class 2 child know by the end of the year?
faq.a: Reading and building numbers to 1000, adding and subtracting two-digit numbers with carrying and borrowing, the 2, 5 and 10 tables, half and quarter of simple shapes, Indian money and change, and telling time to the hour and half-hour.

faq.q: My child understands a topic in the book but forgets it. What helps?
faq.a: This is normal and it is exactly why worksheets exist. A textbook teaches a concept once; a reflex like regrouping needs twenty varied questions, not five. Short daily practice on the same idea for a week fixes it.
